title: Who Is Behind the Australian Centre for the Public Understanding of Education
author: Filling the Pail
summary: This investigative piece traces the anonymous authorship behind a newly launched group, the Australian Centre for the Public Understanding of Education (ACPUE), which published an unsigned critique of a report by the Australian Education Research Organisation (AERO) on evidence-based teaching practices. After receiving no response to a direct inquiry, the author used AI tools, including ChatGPT to surface a since-scrubbed LinkedIn post and Pangram to check AI-authorship of related posts, to build a circumstantial case that Emeritus Professor Robert Hattam of Adelaide University is a founding figure, based on a since-deleted LinkedIn credit, his open hostility to AERO's evidence base, and his prior co-authored academic paper attacking similar 'seminal' research. The piece situates this in a broader institutional conflict: the author argues Australian education academia has produced decades of practically useless research (attitude surveys, theory-heavy papers) and now feels threatened by AERO's classroom-focused, evidence-based advice, making ACPUE's ostensibly neutral 'public understanding' framing a misleading cover for a defensive campaign by the field's old guard.
points: The author's central ethical complaint is that ACPUE presents itself as a neutral, academic 'public understanding' initiative while its founders decline to identify themselves, which he argues breaches the transparency and accountability that academic institutions otherwise insist upon.

AI tools directly aided the investigation: ChatGPT surfaced a LinkedIn post naming Robert Hattam as a founding researcher (a claim its author, Rebecca Burtenshaw, would not elaborate on before blocking the reporter), and the AI-detection tool Pangram flagged one of Hattam's own LinkedIn posts as 100% AI-generated.

Hattam, an Emeritus Professor at Adelaide University, is quoted directly attacking AERO's evidence base as 'bullshit' and accusing it of 'pushing dumbed down teaching,' and had previously co-authored an academic paper attacking similar 'seminal' education research, both cited as circumstantial evidence linking him to ACPUE.

The piece frames the conflict as institutional self-interest: the author argues Australian education academia has a track record of practically useless research (attitude surveys, theory-heavy papers referencing Foucault) and that AERO's classroom-tested, evidence-based advice for teachers 'poses a threat to their ecosystem.'

A second education researcher connected to ACPUE, Rebecca Burtenshaw, is shown through her own published survey research (of 139 maths teachers) espousing scepticism toward students simply 'knowing' mathematical facts and procedures — used by the author as an example of the theoretical, practice-skeptical research culture he says AERO threatens.
quotes: It presents us with a supposedly academic, albeit deeply flawed, critique of a report by the Australian Education Research Organisation.
In contrast, AERO provides practical advice teachers can apply in their own classrooms.
By doing what academics should be doing, AERO poses a threat to their ecosystem.
My biggest problem with AERO .. they're insulting of my whole career as a teacher .. they saunter into our space and claim they have privileged access to THE truth about good teaching.
Pangram appears to be of the view that Hattam's post is 100% AI generated.
So, on the available evidence, it seems reasonable to conclude that Hattam is involved with ACPUE. I am happy to retract this claim if Hattam issues a denial.
Clearly, such research is of no practical value to teachers.
It's not exactly the alien abduction of Elvis, but it's also not standard fare.
